text.p: Swedish truckmaker Scania reported a lower than expected six-month profit on Monday, but upbeat comments about an upturn on the sluggish European truck market in the second half this year helped lift its share price.
Scania's profit after financial items dropped 36 percent to 1.35 billion crowns in the first six months of 1997, short of the 1.43 billion crowns predicted in a Reuter poll of market analysts.
Even so, Scania's chief executive Leif Ostling cheered the stock market by predicting sales recovery in the second half.

"The upturn in demand for heavy trucks which began at the end of the first quarter strengthened during the second quarter," Ostling said, adding that increased order intake would not show in sales until the second half of 1997.
"The market seems to be picking up," he said.
At 1300 GMT, the Scania share was trading five crowns higher at 230 crowns, up five crowns despite a generally soft Stockholm bourse.
"The important thing is that the market seems to be strengthening, so we could see an improvement in the third and fourth quarters," Mats Liss of brokers Swedbank told Reuters.
West European truck order intake rose eight percent in the first six months of the year compared with the same 1996 period and 10 percent in the second quarter from the first quarter, Scania said.

"Order intake was up...and this really confirms what Daimler(-Benz), Volvo and Renault already have showed -- that the European truck market is picking up," said Greg Melich of Brokers Morgan Stanley, adding he expected the truck market to pick up six percent in 1998.
Although analysts were cheered by signs of recovery in Europe, Melich noted that this already was discounted in the share price.
"We think the share is fully valued on these levels and we have a 'neutral' on it," he said.
"We recommend buying Volvo VOLVb.ST because of its car products, restructuring of its North American truck operations and its valuation."
Six-month figures were marked by low sales volumes and continued price pressure in Europe, with prices of Scania's 4-series truck currently one to two percent lower than at this time last year.

Positive currency translation effects helped lift sales to 18.94 billion crowns from 17.38 billion and added 400 million to the operating profit, which nonetheless fell to 1.42 billion from 2.29 billion, depressing the operating margin to 7.5 percent from 13.2 percent for the corresponding period last year.
For the full year, analysts expect profit after financial items to rise to 3.9 billion crowns from 2.71 billion in 1996.
